problem: Crowd counting suffers from occlusion (overlap and invisibility) because datasets and methods use passive, fixed cameras. Embodied navigation methods and datasets are indoor, small-scale, lack Z-axis movement, and have few objects, so they are untested on large dense crowds.
motivation: Occlusion stems from a poor observation point, so an active camera (drone) that optimizes viewpoints could solve it. No task, dataset or method exists for active counting of large outdoor crowds with 6-DoF motion.
key_idea: A zero-shot drone agent uses an MLLM to switch between high- and low-altitude exploration, then computes top-down viewpoints from normal lines of clustered crowd point clouds for fine detection and counting.
insight: Altitude switching cuts travel cost: the ablation without HAE is slightly more accurate (17.46 vs 18.91 MAPE) but travels 4633 m vs 3804 m, while without LAE the error is 88.08. Viewpoint design is critical: removing normal lines, viewpoint selection or ATE-view selection drives MAPE to 92-99% or collapses the reachable-point success rate to 1-8%. Real-world tests show NLBN views beat the pre-NLBN views (GD: 15.17 vs 73.74 MAPE).
method: Task ECC: a drone with RGB-D and pose navigates an unknown large outdoor scene, outputs a person count at stop, and is scored by MAPE and travel distance.
ECCD simulator: Unreal Engine 4, 60 scenes up to 40,000 m² and 50 m height, up to 15,000 people, with crowd counts per block drawn from a Poisson point process with expert-set density.

ATE: GPT-4V looks at a panoramic view and outputs s_t; if s_t>0.5 the drone descends from 80 m HAE (frontier exploration) to 10 m LAE. A density model (GL) output is projected onto the global point cloud to estimate crowd distribution.

NLBN: GMM clustering (cluster size ε=40) of the crowd point cloud, plane fit per cluster for normals, candidate view directions at angle ζ=15° to the normal, choose the one closest to the ATE view vector (obstacle-free), and place the point at η=8 m from the cluster center.
FDC: the drone visits the navigation points, runs Grounding DINO on close-up RGB, projects box centers into 3D via depth, deduplicates in 0.25 m voxels, and counts the targets.

setting.backbone: GPT-4V (frozen) for altitude decisions + Generalized Loss density counter + Grounding DINO detector (pretrained) + geometric planning
setting.embodiment: simulated drone (6-DoF, UE4); real Taobotics Q300 drone in a small real test
setting.observation: RGB-D multi-camera (incl. downward and surrounding panorama) + pose
setting.action_space: 3D navigation waypoints (x,y,z) executed by path planning (A*-style pathfinding)
setting.control: waypoint-by-waypoint; HAE/LAE switching by MLLM, then NLBN waypoints; stops after visiting all waypoints
setting.privileged: none stated (depth and pose from sensors); MVC baselines use densely placed cameras; ground truth is used only for evaluation

resource.name: ECCD (Embodied Crowd Counting Dataset)
resource.scale: 60 UE4 scenes, up to 40,000 m² and 50 m height, up to 15,488 people per scene
resource.tasks: Actively count people in large outdoor scenes without instructions
resource.splits: no official split described; evaluated across scenes and five density levels L1-L5
resource.metrics: MAPE (%), travel distance TD (m), number of cameras for multi-view baselines
resource.headline: ZECC: 18.71 MAPE, 3722.45 m TD (best ZSON baseline CoW+GD: 46.01 MAPE)

results: ZECC reaches 18.71% MAPE at 3722 m travel, versus 46.01-60.57% MAPE for FBE, CoW and OpenFMNav with similar or higher travel cost. It approaches the multi-view methods MVF-10 (15.13) and CountFormer-10 (12.8) using only 5 cameras instead of 1735. The obstructed-person ratio is 4.52% versus 42.81% for OpenFMNav.
limitations: Simulation-only evaluation with static crowds; the real-world test is small (2 scenes) with a rough pipeline
Depends on GPT-4V decisions, which fail when buildings occlude the crowd; relies on pretrained counting and detection models
No learned navigation baselines; baselines are adapted indoor ZSON methods, and hyperparameters are hand-set
